extracted.intended_audience: Canadian patent applicants, patent agents/attorneys, and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_short: unity of invention and new matter
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on Canadian Patent Act/Rules standards for (1) when amendments or divisional filings introduce 'new matter' and (2) assessing 'unity of invention' (one invention only) during examination, including special rules for translations and PCT national phase applications. Aimed at applying the statutory and procedural tests and preparing/responding to examiner reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments must not introduce new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to the specification and drawings may be amended, as long as the amendments, inter alia, do not contain new matter when compared to what was filed originally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an examiner determines that an amended specification or amended drawing includes new matter, the defect will be identified in an examiner’s report and the applicant will be requisitioned to remove the new matter. Amendments containing new matter will also be laid open on the date the application is laid open to public inspection or on the date the amendment is placed on file, whichever is later; this can affect later patentability in Canada or elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable inference standard for English/French-filed applications
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications originally filed in English or French, the specification and drawings may not be amended to describe matter that cannot reasonably be inferred from the specification and drawings as originally filed (subsection 38.2(2) of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is whether the amended matter can 'reasonably be inferred' from the originally filed documents. Note that deletion of originally-filed matter can itself cause non-compliance if, after deletion, the remaining disclosure would not reasonably infer the amended content (example: removal of a specific material recitation could be treated as new matter if it could not be inferred that other materials were intended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding prior-art material requires explicit acknowledgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter pertaining to prior art with respect to the application may be added to the specification and the drawings, however the applicant must acknowledge in the specification that any such matter is prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter admitted as prior art is an exception to the new-matter prohibition, but must be explicitly identified as prior art in the specification to be treated as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter for regularly-filed Canadian applications originally in other languages
rubrics_metrics.description: For regularly-filed Canadian (non-PCT) applications filed in a language other than English or French, amendments must be reasonable to infer from both: (a) the specification and drawings contained in the application on its filing date; and (b) the specification or drawings contained in the application immediately after the text matter is replaced by an English or French translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translated documents submitted under subsection 15(2) or 15(3) of the Patent Rules replace the originally filed specification and drawings; examination of new matter proceeds on the basis of these translated documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter for PCT national phase applications originally in other languages
rubrics_metrics.description: PCT national phase applications filed in a language other than English or French must meet the amendment requirements in subsection 155.6(1) of the Patent Rules: amendments must be reasonable to infer from both (a) the specification and drawings contained in the international application on its filing date; and (b) the translated text matter in the specification and drawings (and any untranslated text matter in a non-language-dependent sequence listing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments cannot be based on untranslated text matter unless those amendments are reasonable to infer from the remainder of the specification/drawings (excluding untranslated terms), or the untranslated terms are present in non-language-dependent free text in the sequence listing. Where same text appears in English/French and another language in the sequence listing, the other language is disregarded for new-matter assessment (subsection 155.6(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of translation errors in PCT national phase applications
rubrics_metrics.description: If an amendment is reasonable to infer from the originally filed PCT international application but is not reasonable to infer from the national phase translated text due to an error in the translation, the translation may be corrected under subsection 155.2(2) of the Patent Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A compliant corrected translation is considered submitted on the date of the original translation and is used for new matter assessment under 155.6(1). However, a failure to translate certain terms is not considered a translation 'error' and cannot be corrected under 155.2(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter assessment for divisional applications at filing/presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of a divisional application is assessed as of its presentation date and compared to the content of the original parent application on its filing date; any matter neither contained in nor reasonably inferable from the original parent application is considered new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analysis applies both on filing of the divisional and when the divisional is amended. Where the parent is itself a divisional, the chain must be traced back to the original parent’s filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on matter in regularly-filed divisional applications (hypothetical addition test)
rubrics_metrics.description: For regularly-filed Canadian (non-PCT) divisional applications, a divisional cannot be filed with matter that could not have been hypothetically added to the specification and/or drawings of the original parent application under section 38.2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every application in a chain of divisionals must be assessed against its original parent; if matter is considered new for any application in the chain it is new for the divisional. If new matter is present and not admitted as prior art, a defect is identified under section 91 of the Patent Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter rules for PCT national phase divisionals (translation considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: For divisional applications of PCT national phase applications, the requirements of section 155.7 of the Patent Rules apply and an analysis must determine whether matter in the divisional, if hypothetically added to the original PCT specification and its translation, would introduce new matter in view of subsection 155.6(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PCT national phase applications may allow corrections to mistranslations, an additional translation-focused analysis is required when assessing divisional content for new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments to divisional applications restricted by original-parent compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection 38.2(3.1) of the Patent Act states that the specification and drawings of a divisional application may not be amended to add matter that (a) could not have been added to the original parent application; and (b) cannot be reasonably inferred from the divisional application at its presentation date. Subsection 38.2(4) provides an exception for matter admitted as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the original parent is itself a divisional, a corresponding chain analysis is required. For PCT national phase divisionals, subsection 155.6(3) requires an analogous analysis allowing for corrections to mistranslations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional rules for divisional applications filed before Oct 30, 2019
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisional applications filed before October 30, 2019 are evaluated based on the subsections 38.2(2) and 38.2(3) of the Patent Act in force as of the date of filing of the divisional application or date of amendment respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments made on or after October 30, 2019 to a divisional filed before that date will be assessed under the rules applicable to amendments (see section 20.04.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention — one invention only (Section 36)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent shall be granted for one invention only. Where an application describes more than one invention, the applicant may limit the claims to one invention only and any other invention disclosed may be made the subject of a divisional application (subsection 36(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is largely procedural—identifying lack of unity does not itself determine patentability; it requires the applicant to elect one invention for prosecution or to file divisionals for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'one invention only' — single general inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of section 36, 'one invention' includes a group of inventions linked in such a manner that they form a single general inventive concept (section 88 of the Patent Rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'invention' in the unity context is broader than the statutory definition in section 2 and can include 'aspects of a single invention'—claims that are so linked form one invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony with PCT unity standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Canadian unity standard is equivalent to the PCT standard: 'one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a single general inventive concept' (Rule 13.1 PCT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canadian practice is not different from or additional to the PCT requirement; PCT guidelines (e.g. WIPO ISPE Guidelines) provide useful examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: General inventive concept — criteria for linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether a 'single general inventive concept' exists linking the claims by considering the purpose of the invention: the claimed invention should provide a solution to a practical problem; claims defining that solution or refinements may relate to a single inventive concept. Generally, a set of claims will share a general inventive concept if a set of new and unobvious elements is common to each claim, provided they are required for proper operation in the invention's broadest aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive concept concerns how a result is obtained (the inventive aspects of a practical solution), not unity of result alone. The PCT expression 'special technical features' refers to novel and unobvious claim elements that define the contribution over the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori and a posteriori unity evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity can be evaluated a priori (presence of a common set of elements among claims, without regard to prior art) and a posteriori (whether the common elements are new and unobvious over the prior art). A lack of unity may be identified by either analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A typical a priori approach: identify the claim with the fewest elements and check if those elements (or corresponding equivalents) appear in all other independent claims. 'Corresponding' elements (equivalents whose roles correspond) can suffice. Prior art relevant to novelty/obviousness may be considered for a posteriori assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure when lack of unity is found
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner identifies lack of unity of invention, the defect is identified in an examiner’s report under subsection 86(2) of the Patent Rules and the applicant is requisitioned to correct it or submit arguments. The report need only identify the unity defect and prosecution of substantive issues may be deferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The applicant has a one-time election to choose the 'one invention only' for examination; claims amended post-election generally must have unity with the elected invention. If the applicant declines to limit claims, the examiner may refer the application to the Commissioner (typically after at least two reports). Commissioner directions under subsection 36(2.1) can require limiting claims; failure to comply may lead to refusal under section 40.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and explanation required in a unity report
rubrics_metrics.description: A report identifying lack of unity should explain the basis to enable the applicant to decide how to limit or divide claims: it should identify what the examiner considers the distinct inventions to be and provide sufficient detail why they do not share a single general inventive concept. For a posteriori defects, prior art supporting the conclusion should be cited and explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, the examiner should relate each identified invention to the specific claims that define it and set out groups of claims deemed to be 'one invention only', indicating which group each independent claim belongs to. Dependent claims are presumed to belong to the group of the claim they refer to unless explicitly indicated otherwise. If a lack of unity exists among alternatives in a single claim, the examiner should, where practical, separate the alternatives into groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for identifying a lack of unity defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, a lack of unity should be identified in the first report written in respect of the claims that lack unity. However, if other defects (e.g. obviousness, ambiguity, lack of utility/support) bear on unity, the unity defect may be formally identified in a later report after advising the applicant that those defects impact unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lack of unity introduced by applicant amendment may be identified regardless of prior examination duration. Where prior art raises the possibility of a posteriori lack of unity but some claims are anticipated/obvious, it may be preferable to resolve prior art defects first before formally identifying unity issues.
